title: Accurate cold forged parts through adjustable dies
abstract: Abstract In response to the growing demands for both sustainability and precision in metal forming, this study investigates the potential of an adaptive die system for cold forging processes. The system allows of control of die preload during the main forming and ejection phases, thus offering two degrees of freedom to influence product properties. Through a combination of experimental and numerical investigations, the interdependence between the final part diameter, axial residual stresses, and ejection forces is systematically analyzed. It is shown that increasing the preload during forming reduces the final diameter. Conversely, preload applied during ejection has a direct influence on the resulting ejection force and surface stresses. This decoupling capability enables targeted tuning of individual product properties. To experimentally represent the variability of material batches, three different steel grades were selected, spanning a broad range of flow stresses. The resulting process maps reveal how fluctuations in material properties affect forming outcomes, and how the adaptive die system can be used to compensate these effects. The experimental trends were confirmed by finite element simulations, which support the physical interpretation of preload-related elastic and plastic interactions within the tooling system. The study shows that adjusting the preload intelligently enables dimensional corrections and residual stress or ejection force optimization. The primary focus is on understanding and modeling the process-property relationships. The results lay the foundation for potential control strategies, such as inline or part-to-part adaptation. These strategies can be integrated into future forming lines for increased robustness and flexibility.

sections.heading: Introduction
paragraphs: Industrial production is under increasing pressure to reduce its ecological footprint while maintaining high product quality and process reliability. International climate strategies define net-zero greenhouse gas emissions by 2050 as a central target [ 4 ]. Similar objectives are reflected in European sustainability and financing strategies [ 35 ]. In Germany, these goals are also anchored in national climate policy [ 3 ]. In this context, the metalworking industry is of particular relevance, as it accounts for approximately 9 % of the total product carbon footprint (PCF) in Germany when all product stages are considered [ 13 ].

Cold forging is a key technology in metal processing, but its ecological impact is mainly determined by upstream and downstream process steps rather than by the forming operation itself. For standardized machine screws, for example, up to 66 % of the total PCF can be attributed to the production of the input stock, whereas 28.3 % results from the overall thermal treatment within the entire process chain, including subsequent quenching and tempering [ 11 ]. In contrast, the actual cold forming operation contributes less than 5 % to the total PCF. Accordingly, reducing material-related emissions, avoiding unnecessary heat treatment steps, and improving the resource efficiency of the process chain are promising approaches for lowering the environmental impact of cold-forged components.

However, these sustainability-oriented approaches may conflict with the strict requirements for dimensional accuracy, mechanical performance, and functional product properties in cold forging [ 24 ]. Previous studies have shown that comparable hardness levels can be achieved by adapting material selection and process parameters, even when conventional heat treatment routes are modified [ 47 ]. However, omitting or reducing of thermal treatment may leave residual stresses in the component that would otherwise be relieved during heat treatment [ 6 ]. Such residual stress states can affect dimensional stability during subsequent manufacturing steps and are also relevant for fatigue performance [ 50 ].

A second sustainability-related challenge arises from the increasing use of low-carbon or recycled steel. Green steel offers considerable potential for reducing carbon-intensive primary steel production [ 12 ]. Electric-arc-furnace-based steelmaking is therefore regarded as an important route toward lower-emission steel production [ 43 ]. However, scrap-based production routes can introduce residual alloying elements, with copper being one of the most critical elements for cold forming applications. Copper can promote segregation and precipitation phenomena and thereby affect microstructural stability [ 7 ]. Its influence on the mechanical response and formability of steels has also been reported in metallurgical investigations [ 30 ]. Similar effects have been observed for stainless steels, where copper additions can influence deformation behavior and formability [ 16 ]. As a consequence, copper-related embrittlement may increase the risk of crack initiation during cold forming [ 40 ]. At the same time, the growing demand for copper, particularly due to electrification and electric mobility, makes a complete avoidance of copper contamination in recycled steel increasingly challenging [ 37 ].

Fig. 1 Experimental investigation of the achievable dimensional accuracy in the forming zone during a diameter reduction process from 13 mm to 12 mm: ( a ) results obtained with low preload in the forming die and ( b ) results obtained with high preload in the forming die. The horizontal lines indicate the corresponding ISO tolerance grades.

The underlying mechanism is the elastic behavior of the tool–workpiece system. A change in material flow stress directly affects the required forming force and thus the elastic deformation and springback of the die [ 32 ]. Depending on tool stiffness and process design, elastic springback can reach several hundred micrometers [ 33 ]. Stochastic analyses of cold forging processes have also shown that material and process variations can significantly influence dimensional accuracy [ 23 ]. Since tight tolerances are essential for the functionality, reliability, and safety of cold-forged components, even small material-induced deviations can become technologically relevant [ 31 ]. These findings show that conventional cold forging processes, despite their generally high robustness, have only limited adaptability to fluctuations in material behavior. To meet the combined demands of sustainability and precision, adaptive process monitoring and control strategies are therefore required [ 8 ].

This study addresses this challenge by investigating an adaptive die system for cold forging. The core idea is to introduce controllable flexibility into the tool system by adjusting the die preload during the forming cycle. Unlike conventional dies, where the preload is defined during assembly and remains constant, the adaptive concept enables the preload to be varied independently during the main forming phase and the ejection phase. By modifying the preload during forming, the elastic expansion of the die can be influenced and dimensional deviations can be compensated, as illustrated in Fig.  1 b. By modifying the preload during ejection, an additional degree of freedom is introduced to affect ejection forces and residual stress states. The specific focus of this paper is the experimental and numerical analysis of the cause–effect relationships between die preload, forming force, final diameter, ejection force, and axial residual stresses. A deliberately simple axisymmetric reduction geometry is used to isolate these fundamental relationships. The investigated materials are not intended to represent typical batch-to-batch scatter of a single steel grade. Instead, they define a broadened material-property window to assess whether the adaptive die system can compensate material-induced changes in product properties under strongly varying forming conditions. Based on the resulting process maps, the potential of adaptive die systems for future closed-loop control strategies in precision cold forging is discussed.

sections.heading: Geometrical tolerance
paragraphs: The achievable dimensional precision in cold forging is commonly classified using ISO tolerance grades. Under optimized conditions, cold-forged parts can reach accuracies up to IT7 [ 2 ]. Comparable precision limits are also reported in standard forming technology literature [ 22 ]. Such tolerances are not only relevant for quality assurance, but directly affect component functionality. For cold-forged transmission shafts, tighter tolerances can increase the maximum transmittable torque in interference-fit shaft–hub connections [ 29 ]. In gear manufacturing, insufficient flank accuracy can reduce efficiency or lead to undesirable meshing effects [ 15 ]. In turbomachinery, increased blade tip clearance promotes leakage losses and can reduce stage efficiency [ 18 ].

Dimensional deviations in cold forging are mainly caused by the elastic deflection of the tool and workpiece during forming [ 24 ]. Springback during unloading and ejection can further modify the final geometry [ 32 ]. The accuracy of reduced diameters is influenced by workpiece and tool geometry, flow stress, Young’s modulus, forming work, press stiffness, thermal effects, and friction. Within the framework of Eq.  1 , these factors can be assigned to the domains  X ,  V , and  W .

Previous analytical and numerical studies have shown that dimensional accuracy results from the coupled interaction of material behavior, tool stiffness, thermal effects, and tribology. Long et al. demonstrated that cooling after springback contributes significantly to dimensional deviations in forward extrusion [ 27 ]. Further finite element studies confirmed the relevance of elastic and thermal effects for dimensional errors in extrusion processes [ 25 ]. Similar dependencies were also reported for backward cup extrusion [ 26 ]. In addition, longer calibration zones in the die can increase radial deviations in the final geometry [ 49 ]. These findings show that geometrical tolerances in cold forging are highly sensitive to variations in the process chain and motivate adaptive tooling concepts that allow the target geometry to be influenced during production.

sections.heading: Forming strategies used in cold forging
paragraphs: Flexible forming strategies in cold forging aim to extend conventional process control by introducing additional motions or force-controlled degrees of freedom. Such strategies are used to influence a target property  Y  during forming and can therefore be understood as active process control concepts [ 1 ]. In contrast, passive strategies mainly modify the tool or process setup before forming in order to improve robustness.

Most early approaches were passive and used measured or simulated deviations to adapt the tool geometry. Jütte showed that cemented carbide dies reduce elastic springback due to their higher Young’s modulus, thereby modifying the forming system  W  [ 21 ]. Schmieder demonstrated by finite element analysis that high-precision tool manufacturing and minimized tool deviations are essential for achieving high part quality in cold forging [ 39 ]. Although such approaches improve robustness, their ability to actively adjust product properties during production remains limited.

Further strategies use axially displaceable punches in multi-stage cold forging. Tchasse demonstrated an adaptive punch system that continuously corrects the head height of screw blanks over several forming stages [ 44 ]. By using regression-based learning, the punch stroke was adjusted during the process chain, enabling compensation of thermal fluctuations and improving the robustness of the final head geometry.

Besides dimensional accuracy, active forming strategies can also be used to influence process forces and material-related product properties. Obermaier investigated combined extrusion of aluminum using an axially movable die and showed that a co-moving die can improve local friction conditions and reduce process forces [ 34 ]. Hoche et al. used the ejector as a counterpunch during solid forward extrusion and demonstrated that higher counterforces promote a more homogeneous plastic deformation, thereby reducing near-surface tensile residual stresses [ 14 ]. In a different tool concept, Franceschi et al. investigated an active die system in which a conically reinforced die was coupled to a draw cushion to modulate the radial die preload during ejection [ 6 ]. Using this active die, they showed that increasing the die preload during ejection can reduce forming-induced residual stresses in the component.

However, the state of the art also indicates that most existing forming strategies focus on one dominant process variable or product property, such as dimensional accuracy, process force, or residual stress. In practical process control, these quantities are not independent but change simultaneously. Consequently, a reliable adjustment of adaptive tooling systems requires a comprehensive understanding of the interactions between tool preload, forming force, ejection force, final geometry, and residual stress state.

sections.heading: Objectives and approach
paragraphs: Previous studies have shown that using an adaptive die system with controllable radial preload on the die insert can significantly influence both the residual stress distribution and the ejection forces in cold forging [ 47 ]. These investigations have so far concentrated primarily on adjusting the preload during the ejection phase, aiming to reduce mechanical loading during part removal and to tailor near-surface plastic deformation for improved residual stress profiles [ 6 ]. However, preliminary results, as illustrated in Fig.  1 , indicate that modifying the preload during the main forming stroke can also affect the final diameter after reduction during cold forward extrusion, thereby expanding the functional potential of the adaptive tooling concept.

This study therefore analyzes how the two available degrees of freedom, defined as the controlled application of preload during forming and during ejection, can be used to influence not only geometric tolerances but also secondary variables such as residual stresses and ejection forces. The central focus lies in establishing the correlation between the adjustable axial feed force, which governs the radial preload, and the three identified target variables. In addition, the sensitivity of each output variable to changes in process conditions is evaluated to assess the predictability and controllability of the system. Fig. 2 Illustration of the active die integrated within the tooling system, which is installed in a multi-action press: ( a ) active die design based on a segmented sleeve and an axially movable conical reinforcement, ( b ) tooling system, and ( c ) spindle press setup Fig. 3 Numerical representation of the axial infeed motion of the active die and the resulting generation of compressive stresses in the die insert as a function of the required infeed force

To investigate these correlations and dependencies, a comprehensive experimental study was carried out using three steels with distinctly different flow stresses. Rather than representing typical batch-to-batch scatter of a single steel grade, these materials define a broadened material-property window to analyze the transferability of the effects resulting from preload variations during the main forming and ejection phases. This allows the study to assess whether material-induced changes in product properties, such as those caused by varying flow behavior in green steel, can be compensated by the adaptive die system. Each material variant was subjected to forward extrusion of a reduced-diameter geometry under defined preload conditions, while a numerical model was used to extend the dataset beyond the experimental constraints. Since the sensitivity to preload adjustment changes with the material, the resulting material-dependent process response represents a central scientific focus of this work. Fig. 4 Infeed curves of the experimental setup from preliminary trials: ( a ) force–displacement curves for different configurations and ( b ) detailed view of the effective infeed range from 0 mm to 2.5 mm

sections.heading: Description of the process
paragraphs: As illustrated in Fig.  4 a, the measured force–displacement behavior reveals a distinct sequence of mechanical interactions within the adaptive tooling system. Between 0 mm and 1 mm of axial displacement, the total force increases to approximately 200 kN due to the restoring action of the integrated gas springs. This effect occurs regardless of whether the die insert is present. From 1.5 mm to 4 mm, no significant increase in axial force is observed, as this range is primarily associated with the elimination of mechanical play between the active reinforcement, the segmented sleeve, and the die insert. During this interval, no effective radial expansion of the die takes place. Only beyond an axial displacement of 4 mm does the system begin to transmit axial force into radial pressure on the die insert. This is evidenced by a divergence in the force–displacement curves with and without the die. The difference between both curves defines the effective preload force exerted by the active reinforcement, as indicated by the red curve in Fig.  4 b.

In the experiment, an axial displacement of 2.5 mm results in a total preload force of approximately 300 kN, which corresponds to the maximum force capacity of the draw cushion used in this study. This maximum force defines the upper operational limit of the system. Consequently, the effective operating range for the draw cushion is constrained between approximately 200 kN and 300 kN in the experimental data shown in Fig.  4 a, which corresponds to a range of 0 kN to 100 kN in the simulated force–displacement behavior presented in Fig.  4 b. This force window serves as the practical basis for the die preload modulation applied during the subsequent forming trials.

The individual steps of the forming process with inline-controlled preload modulation are illustrated in Fig.  5 , highlighting six key stages. To facilitate understanding of how the adaptive preload is varied throughout the forming cycle, the corresponding force–displacement profile of the draw cushion, as measured during the experimental trials, is shown alongside the process steps. In Step 1, an initial preload is applied by axially advancing the active reinforcement, establishing a defined radial clamping pressure on the die insert. Two preload levels were investigated for the forming phase: a high-preload state, corresponding to a draw cushion displacement of 5.75 mm and a force of approximately 80 kN, and a low-preload state, defined by a displacement of 4 mm and negligible preload force of approximately 0 kN.

The forming stage begins in Steps 2 and 3 with the downward motion of the main punch, which progressively reduces the specimen to its target diameter. Plastic deformation initiates in Step 3 and is accompanied by a moderate rise in the force recorded on the draw cushion, as illustrated in Fig.  6 b. This behavior is attributed to the internal redistribution of process forces: as deformation progresses, a portion of the punch force is transmitted through the draw cushion. Since the draw cushion maintains a fixed axial position during forming, an additional preload force is required to counterbalance this transmission and ensure position stability throughout the forming stroke.

At bottom dead center, a short dwell time is introduced to allow adjustment of the die preload, as shown in Step 5. Three preload levels were defined for this phase: a high preload of nearly 100 kN at 6.25 mm displacement, a medium preload of 75 kN at 5.75 mm, and a low preload of 0 kN at 4 mm. Finally, in Step 6, the part is ejected by retracting the main punch. This phase requires a defined ejection force, which is influenced by the residual preload state in the die. As summarized in Fig.  6 b, both the preload during forming and the preload during ejection were varied independently as part of a parametric study. This dual-stage preload adjustment yields two degrees of freedom for process control, providing the basis for the investigations presented in this work.

sections.heading: Numerical setup
paragraphs: To model the forming process with adaptive preload modulation, the numerical framework illustrated in Fig.  7  was implemented. Two different model configurations were employed to capture the process behavior. A two-dimensional axisymmetric model was developed to exploit the rotational symmetry of the reducing operation. This approach enables computationally efficient simulation of the full forming process, including adaptive die actuation, within approximately one hour. The 2D setup allows for systematic variation of material properties, friction conditions, and process parameters across a wide range of input combinations. To additionally account for the mechanical compliance introduced by the axial slits in the segmented sleeve shown in Fig.  2 a, a three-dimensional finite element model of the same forming process was created. Both 2D and 3D simulations were performed using Simufact Forming 2024.4 with an implicit solver. In order to accurately capture the elastic recovery of the die insert during forming and ejection, as well as the mechanical effects of variable preload, the die and segmented sleeve were modeled as deformable elastic bodies without plasticity. The conical outer reinforcement sleeve was modeled as a rigid body. Fig. 7 Overview of the 2D FE model used for numerical parameter studies, highlighting the key components and material properties

sections.heading: Transformation from 2D to 3D
paragraphs: To reduce computational time and facilitate the generation of large and diverse datasets, the parametric simulations in this study were primarily conducted using a 2D axisymmetric model. However, this simplification introduces discrepancies in the radial mechanical response, particularly in how the axial infeed force translates into radial die contraction. Due to the absence of segmented geometry in the conical sleeve within the 2D model, a higher axial force is required to achieve the same radial reduction of the die’s inner diameter as in the full 3D case. Figure  8  illustrates this deviation by comparing selected simulations, where the axial forces required to reach equivalent levels of radial die shrinkage are shown for both 2D and 3D configurations. Importantly, identical boundary conditions were applied across all simulations, including consistent friction coefficients and material models. Despite these uniform settings, the 2D simulations consistently exhibit a higher axial force demand. This effect is attributed to the increased mechanical stiffness caused by the absence of segmentation in the sleeve, which prevents localized deformation and stress relief.

sections.heading: Calibration of the FE model
Process forces
paragraphs: Figure  10 a presents the experimental and numerical results of the punch force as a function of the infeed force applied during the main forming stage. In this context, the infeed force is used as an indirect measure of die preload, where values near −100 kN correspond to high radial confinement, while values close to 0 kN represent minimal preload. Among the tested materials, the austenitic stainless steel 1.4404 exhibits the highest punch forces, both experimentally and numerically. This behavior is attributed to its higher flow stress and elevated friction coefficient compared to the case-hardening steel 1.7131 and the structural steel 1.0577. The experimental error bars reveal no statistically significant variation in punch force across different preload levels. This finding is consistent with the FE simulations, which similarly show that the radial preload applied during the main forming stroke has only a negligible influence on punch force. The reason lies in the very small geometric changes induced by preload variation. Reductions in the die inner diameter remain within the micrometer range and are therefore insufficient to measurably affect the overall flow resistance during forming. Outliers observed in the experimental data, especially for 1.7131, are consequently not interpreted as a systematic consequence of varying preload. Instead, they are more likely caused by uncontrolled process fluctuations, such as local differences in material condition, lubrication, or surface preparation. These effects introduce experimental scatter but do not alter the core finding: die preload during forming has no meaningful impact on punch force.

Figure  10 b illustrates the influence of preload variation on ejection forces. Here, the preload change is defined as the difference between the infeed force during forming and during ejection. A positive value indicates a reduction of preload after forming, whereas a negative value denotes an increase. Several key observations can be drawn. Even without changing the preload, a baseline ejection force is required to overcome the residual clamping pressure caused by elastic springback of both the part and the tooling. Increasing the preload during ejection intensifies this clamping effect and leads to higher ejection forces. Conversely, reducing the preload significantly lowers the required force for part removal. This trend is consistently observed across all material variants, with stainless steel again exhibiting the highest absolute ejection forces due to its higher flow stress and friction level.

The numerical contact analysis confirms that higher die infeed forces result in increased contact pressure at the die–component interface, thereby explaining the elevated ejection forces. Reducing the preload alleviates this mechanical interlock and thus facilitates easier ejection. The experimental data further suggest the existence of a material-specific preload level at which the ejection force approaches zero. The FE simulations reproduce the qualitative trend but exhibit a more pronounced quadratic decrease in ejection force compared to the approximately linear experimental behavior. This deviation is mainly attributed to the use of a constant Coulomb friction coefficient in the numerical model. In reality, the ejection stage represents a distinct tribological load case because sliding direction is reversed after the lubricant film has already been mechanically and thermally preloaded during the main forming stroke.

Recent tribological investigations using a two-stage sliding compression test have shown that, for polymer-based single-layer lubricants, the effective friction coefficient in the reverse stroke can decrease when the contact pressure is reduced [ 42 ]. This pressure-dependent response is not immediately intuitive, since common friction trends for the main forming stroke often report a decrease in apparent friction with increasing contact pressure [ 10 ]. At the same time, reducing the contact pressure during ejection also lowers the local thermal and mechanical load acting on the already preloaded lubricant film. Two complementary hypotheses can therefore be used to explain the observed behavior. First, unloading may support partial recovery or homogenization of the separation layer, resulting in a more uniform lubricant film in the contact zone. Second, polymer-based lubricant systems may exhibit a reversal of their temperature-dependent behavior once a critical thermal load has been exceeded [ 10 ]. While moderate heating can reduce lubricant viscosity and thus lower friction, excessive thermal loading during the preceding forward stroke can impair the performance of the polymer film [ 28 ]. In this case, lowering the contact pressure before the reverse stroke reduces further thermal degradation and leads to a lower effective friction coefficient during ejection. Consequently, the reduction in ejection force caused by decreasing die preload is not only a result of lower mechanical clamping pressure but can additionally be amplified by a simultaneous decrease in the local friction coefficient [ 42 ]. Fig. 11 Evaluation of experimentally measured diameters in the forming zone for three different materials, based on a target reference diameter of 11.995 mm: ( a ) results for 1.4404, ( b ) results for 1.7131, ( c ) results for 1.0577, and ( d ) visualization of the measurement setup using the Keyence TM-X5040 system

sections.heading: Local diameter variation
paragraphs: Consequently, preload adjustment during forming is more effective for controlling the final diameter, whereas preload adjustment during ejection primarily influences the ejection force. This interpretation is supported by both the experimental and numerical results, which show the same fundamental trend with only minor quantitative deviations.

Another key finding is the influence of material properties on the final diameter. A comparison of Fig.  11 a–c shows that materials with higher flow stresses generally result in larger final diameters when the die geometry remains unchanged. This behavior can be explained by the higher forming forces and contact normal stresses required to plastically deform these materials. The increased contact pressure causes stronger elastic expansion of the die cavity during forming. After unloading and ejection, this elastic tool deformation affects the final component geometry and leads to larger resulting diameters. This trend is clearly visible when comparing 1.4404 and 1.7131 to 1.0577, and it is evident in both the experimental and numerical results.

A less distinct behavior is observed for 1.7131, which shows diameter changes comparable to those of 1.4404 despite its lower flow stress, see Fig.  11 b. This indicates that the final diameter cannot be explained by the flow curve alone. Since the observed diameter changes are in the micrometer range, small differences in material condition and process response can have a measurable influence. Possible contributing factors include material-related uncertainties in 1.7131, such as local variations in homogeneity, anisotropy, or batch-specific differences in the mechanical response. These effects may influence the local springback behavior and can make the trend less distinct than would be expected from the flow stress level alone. In addition, differences in tribological behavior may have a secondary influence on the final geometry. Under identical lubrication conditions, 1.7131 exhibits a lower friction coefficient than 1.4404, see Table  1 . This may lead to slightly reduced contact temperatures and altered contact conditions during forming and unloading. Although this effect is expected to be subordinate compared to the influence of flow stress and die expansion, it can still contribute to small deviations in the micrometer range. Therefore, the comparable diameter response of 1.7131 and 1.4404 is interpreted as the result of a superposition of material scatter, local springback behavior, and tribological effects rather than as a purely flow-stress-controlled phenomenon.

In summary, the results indicate that the combination of preload levels during the forming and ejection phases can be used to actively tune the resulting component diameter. The decisive factor is the independent adjustment of die preload in both process phases. This enables the final geometry to be shifted within the micrometer range and provides an additional degree of freedom for compensating material-induced diameter deviations.

sections.heading: Residual stresses vs. ejection forces
paragraphs: In addition to the observed variations in final diameter and ejection force, the use of an actively controlled die system also affects the residual stress state induced during forming. Building upon the findings of Franceschi et al., it has been shown that particularly the preload applied during the ejection phase can significantly influence the residual stress state within the formed components [ 6 ]. Experimental and numerical studies have demonstrated that increasing the die preload during ejection can introduce more pronounced compressive residual stresses near the surface in the deformation zone [ 5 ]. Such compressive residual stresses are known to improve several performance-related properties, including fatigue strength, dimensional stability, and resistance to stress corrosion cracking [ 47 ]. Fig. 12 Correlation between axial surface residual stresses, averaged over different depth regions, and the mean ejection forces obtained from FE simulations

To investigate these effects, residual stresses from FE simulations conducted under varying preload configurations during the forming and ejection phases were analyzed. The simulation series used 1.4404 as the reference material, while friction conditions, material model, and tool and billet geometry were kept constant according to the methodological setup. Only the preload settings during the main forming and ejection phases were varied, and the resulting ejection forces and residual stress values were summarized in Fig.  12 . The figure highlights the correlation between ejection forces and residual stresses at different profile depths in the deformation zone. The residual stresses were evaluated at defined depths below the component surface to ensure comparability between the different preload configurations. The results reveal a clear inverse correlation: higher ejection forces, caused by increased preload during the ejection phase, lead to lower residual stress values and thus to a more compressive residual stress state within the component. Fig. 13 Summary of contour maps based on experimental data for material 1.4404 from nine reference points: ( a ) ejection forces, ( b ) final diameter in the deformation zone, ( c ) axial residual stresses, and ( d ) IT tolerances according to ISO

Consistent with the interpretation by Franceschi et al., this effect can be explained by a secondary forming event occurring during ejection [ 9 ]. Elevated clamping forces during part removal promote additional near-surface plastic deformation, thereby shifting the residual stress state toward compression. The observed relationship allows the residual stress state to be approximated as a function of the ejection force using a second-order polynomial. However, this correlation is not a generally valid material law, but a process-specific calibration for the investigated forming setup. In particular, friction conditions, flow stress, tool and workpiece geometry, and material-dependent phenomena such as deformation-induced martensite formation can shift the relationship between ejection force and residual stress state [ 19 ,  20 ]. An increase in flow stress generally leads to higher forming forces and stronger elastic expansion of the die during forming, which can increase the contact pressure during unloading and ejection. Similarly, an increased friction coefficient raises the resistance that must be overcome during part removal and therefore contributes to higher ejection forces [ 20 ].

At the same time, these parameters also affect the generation of forming-induced residual stresses. Jobst and Merklein showed that the material delivery condition and the resulting material behavior influence the residual stress state after forward rod extrusion [ 19 ]. In addition, Jobst et al. demonstrated that tribological conditions affect material flow and residual stress formation in forward rod extrusion [ 20 ]. Higher friction coefficients promote a more inhomogeneous material flow and stronger near-surface plastic deformation, while higher flow stresses increase the elastic stresses stored in the tool–workpiece system at the same reduction ratio. Consequently, the polynomial correlation shown in Fig.  12  must always be interpreted in relation to the known process conditions and cannot be transferred directly to other materials, lubrication systems, geometries, or preload ranges without recalibration. After such process-specific calibration, ejection force measurements, which are comparatively easy to acquire inline, may provide an indirect indicator of residual stress trends. These trends would otherwise require time-consuming experimental methods such as hole-drilling or X-ray diffraction. Nevertheless, this indirect evaluation does not replace dedicated residual stress measurements for general process validation.

This relationship also reveals a fundamental trade-off. While high ejection forces promote beneficial compressive residual stresses and may therefore improve product performance, they also impose increased mechanical loads on the tooling system. Conversely, reducing the preload during ejection lowers the ejection force, which can improve tool life in high-cycle production scenarios, but may result in less favorable residual stress conditions. This highlights the need for a balanced process design that considers both workpiece quality and tooling durability. Fig. 14 Summary of contour maps based on numerical data for material 1.4404: ( a ) ejection forces, ( b ) final diameter in the deformation zone, ( c ) axial residual stresses, and ( d ) IT tolerances according to ISO

sections.heading: Mapping of process responses
paragraphs: Building on the previous analysis of individual response variables, the influence of different die preload configurations can be visualized in the form of two-dimensional process maps. These maps, constructed for the material 1.4404, illustrate how key output variables such as final diameter, ejection force, and residual stress state respond simultaneously to the die preload applied during the main forming and ejection phases. The experimental results used to generate these contour maps are presented in Fig.  13 . In the case of diameter-related maps, the IT tolerances introduced earlier are also included for reference.

Although the contour maps are based on interpolation, they clearly confirm the trends and correlations identified in the previous sections. For instance, the lowest diameters in the deformation zone are observed for configurations with high preload during both forming and ejection, whereas the largest diameters are found in regions with minimal preload in both phases. In contrast, the highest ejection forces and the lowest, and thus most compressive, residual stresses are obtained when the preload during forming is minimized and subsequently increased during ejection, as shown in Fig.  13 a and c.

A key feature of these process maps is their ability to visualize the interplay between multiple objectives. Since each point in the map corresponds to a specific combination of main-forming and ejection-phase preload, shifting from one operating point to another inevitably alters all associated process responses. However, intelligent trajectory planning within the map can allow selective tuning of individual outcomes. For example, moving from Case 1 to Case 2 along a contour line in Fig.  13 a keeps the ejection force and residual stress approximately constant, while selectively modifying the final diameter and thus the geometric tolerance of the part. This decoupling capability, enabled by active preload control in two independent process phases, provides additional degrees of freedom for process optimization.

Figure  14  presents the corresponding contour maps derived from the numerical simulation results for material 1.4404. Overall, the simulated maps confirm the trends observed in the experimental data in Fig.  13 , as evidenced by the direction and spacing of the contour lines across all target variables. Specifically, higher preload during the main forming phase leads to increased ejection forces and more compressive residual stresses in the final part. Similarly, a combination of high preload during both forming and ejection results in smaller final diameters in the deformation zone.

In summary, while the absolute agreement between experimental and numerical results should be interpreted with caution due to model simplifications and measurement limitations, both sets of process maps consistently reveal the same underlying physical relationships. In particular, they demonstrate how the active die system can be used to tailor key part properties, including geometric tolerances, residual stresses, and process forces, by independently adjusting the preload during different phases of the forming process.

sections.heading: Discussion
paragraphs: The results demonstrate that the two controllable preload phases of the adaptive die system do not affect the process and product properties in the same way. Increasing the die preload during the main forming stage primarily influences the final part diameter, whereas its effect on the punch force remains negligible. This can be explained by the small magnitude of the preload-induced die contraction, which is sufficient to shift the final geometry in the micrometer range but too small to measurably alter the overall forming resistance. In contrast, preload variation during ejection directly affects the mechanical clamping state between part and die. A reduction of preload lowers the residual contact pressure and therefore decreases the ejection force, while an increase in preload intensifies the clamping condition and promotes additional near-surface plastic deformation. Consequently, the adaptive die system provides two functionally different degrees of freedom: one that is more effective for dimensional correction during forming and one that is more relevant for controlling ejection forces and residual stress states during part removal.

A central implication of the process maps is that the target variables cannot be controlled independently by changing a single preload value. Each operating point represents a specific combination of final diameter, ejection force, and residual stress state. Thus, shifting the preload configuration inevitably changes several process responses at the same time. This creates a multi-objective control problem. Increasing the preload during ejection can improve the compressive residual stress state, but it also increases the mechanical load on the tool system. Reducing the preload can reduce ejection forces and tool loading, but it may lead to less favorable residual stresses. At the same time, the two independently adjustable preload phases provide the possibility to partially decouple these effects. For example, a suitable change of the forming-phase preload can be used to adjust the final diameter, while the ejection-phase preload can be selected to balance residual stress modification and ejection force. Process maps therefore represent more than just a visualization of experimental and numerical results. They form the basis for model-based process planning and future closed-loop control strategies.

sections.heading: Conclusions and future work
paragraphs: This study demonstrated the potential of an adaptive die system to compensate for uncertainties in material properties during cold forging. In this work, these uncertainties were experimentally represented by three steels with distinctly different mechanical properties, which were analyzed using a combination of experiments and numerical simulations. The effects of independently controlled preload forces during the main forming and ejection phases were systematically investigated. The objective was to evaluate whether such a system can mitigate quality losses caused by variations in material batches, for example increased flow stress resulting from residual alloying elements in green steel.

Based on the combined experimental and numerical results, several key mechanisms were identified that apply across the investigated material spectrum:  Flow curve identification from the pre-compression stage:  The pre-compression stage of the combined sliding compression test was used to identify the material flow curves by evaluating the axial force-displacement response through FEM-supported inverse parameter identification. This separates the mechanical calibration during upsetting from the subsequent sliding phase used for friction characterization, while effects of initial yielding, such as Lüders strain, were considered in the early plastic deformation range. Preload during forming has negligible influence on punch force:  The radial preload applied during the main forming phase has no significant effect on the punch force. This simplifies inline monitoring, since the punch force can be interpreted primarily as a response to material properties and friction conditions without being substantially affected by the chosen preload level. Preload reduction governs ejection force:  The ejection force is mainly determined by the change in preload between the forming and ejection phases. Experimental data indicate that a sufficiently large preload reduction can reduce the ejection force almost to zero. The FE simulations reproduce this trend qualitatively, although the numerical results show a different curvature due to simplified friction assumptions during the ejection stage. Combined preload improves dimensional accuracy:  The smallest final diameters were obtained when high preload was applied during both forming and ejection. This indicates that the total elastic deformation state of the tool system is decisive for dimensional control and that active preload adjustment can be used to compensate for material-induced diameter deviations. Residual stresses correlate with ejection force:  Due to additional near-surface plastic deformation during ejection, the ejection force correlates with the induced residual stress state. This relationship was found to follow a second-order polynomial trend, indicating that ejection force measurements may serve as an indirect process-specific indicator for residual stress development after suitable calibration. Two degrees of freedom enable multivariate process control:  The independent adjustment of preload during the forming and ejection phases enables partially decoupled control of dimensional tolerance, residual stress state, and ejection force. This allows different product properties to be targeted simultaneously by selecting suitable preload combinations for the respective process phase. Overall, the results confirm that the adaptive die system is capable of compensating for material-related deviations and can serve as a basis for process–property control in cold forging. The numerical results, based on simplified 2D models and constant friction assumptions, were sufficiently accurate to describe the key physical phenomena. The transformation from 2D to 3D, as well as the use of material models derived from tribological testing, proved suitable for analyzing the functional relationships that govern the system behavior. Nevertheless, future research must address several limitations to improve the predictive capability and industrial applicability of the proposed method. More accurate material and friction models are required for numerical simulations that represent real process conditions more faithfully. Particular attention should be given to the friction behavior during the ejection phase, where reversed sliding direction, contact-pressure history, thermal preloading, and time-dependent lubricant behavior play a critical role. Further tribological studies on polymer-based single-layer lubricant systems are therefore necessary to derive suitable friction models that account for the transition from forming to ejection [ 42 ]. In addition, extending the simulation framework from 2D to 3D would improve the representation of segmented tool compliance, elastic springback, and local contact conditions.

Beyond these model improvements, artificial intelligence offers new opportunities for developing predictive control strategies. Machine learning algorithms trained on numerical and experimental process data could be used to generate surrogate models that describe complex input–output relationships across the entire process window [ 41 ]. Such models would enable real-time decision-making in production and allow adaptive process configurations based on changing system parameters, such as geometry, material strength, tribology, and tooling wear. Ultimately, AI-enhanced process models could be integrated into smart manufacturing systems, thereby validating the effectiveness of adaptive tooling concepts for next-generation cold forging applications.
